articleTitle: On the geometry of phasor multiplication
abstract: A full geometrical construction is given for the multiplication of two phasors.

articleTitle: SWITCAP: A switched-capacitor network analysis program part I: Basic features
abstract: The user aspects of a switched-capacitor network analysis program, SWITCAP, are discussed. The relation of the program's simulation facilities (such as frequency-domain analysis, time-domain analysis, and sampling functions) to actual laboratory measurement setups incorporating function generators, oscilloscopes, and spectrum analyzers is described in detail. Some examples illustrating the basic features of the program are also given.

articleTitle: SWITCAP: A switched-capacitor network analysis program part II: Advanced applications
abstract: For pt.I see ibid., vol.5, no.3, p.4-10 (1983). The authors discuss the applications of a general switched-capacitor network (SCN) analysis program called SWITCAP for simulating SCNs containing continuous signal paths, clock feedthrough, resistors, finite-bandwidth amplifiers, and/or many phases.

articleTitle: The Gaver-Stehfest algorithm for approximate inversion of Laplace transforms
abstract: An approximate technique for the inversion of Laplace transforms is represented and some simple applications are given. The limitations of the method were explored and it is clear that functions which have oscillatory inverses present difficulty for the method. Better approximations result from the use of computers with longer word lengths and there is considerable improvement when an averaging algorithm is employed. Eight-bit microcomputers are generally sufficiently accurate for nonoscillatory time functions but transforms for lightly damped sinusoids and Bessel functions require large main-frame computers with relatively long word length.

Two novel active compensated noninverting and inverting finite gain amplifier circuits are reported. Compensation is achieved by using two extra operational amplifiers and four resistors. The proposed amplifiers have negligible phase and magnitude errors over a prescribed frequency range. The inverting amplifier has the attractive advantage of an infinite input impedance. The design equations are given.

articleTitle: History of the circuits and systems society
abstract: THE IEEE CIRCUITS AND SYSTEMS SOCIETY began as The Institute of Radio Engineers' Circuit Theory Group in 1949. Twenty-six IRE members signed a petition dated March 22, which was approved by the Board on April 5, 1949. When the IRE merged with the AIEE, there was also a Committee on Electronic Circuits and Systems within the AIEE. At the time of the merger, the AIEE committee joined the IRE group to become the Professional Technical Group on Circuit Theory of the new IEEE. The official merger agreement between the two parties was dated April 3, 1964. The final revised agreement was approved on December 16, 1964, with the merger to take effect on January 1, 1965. In December 1971, the Circuit Theory Group petitioned for Society status and to call itself the Circuits and Systems Society. This operation took place as a two-step process. The petition to change to Society status was approved by the IEEE Board of Directors in May 1972. At that time, it became the IEEE Circuit Theory Society. Then, in December 1972, the Board approved the name change to the present IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

articleTitle: Gain-bandwidth product effects on SC filters including a quasi-optimal topology
abstract: The gain-bandwidth product (GB) effects on switched-capacitor (SC) filters are analyzed and described in detail. A systematic general analysis method is reviewed. To biquad SC filters with the same ideal transfer function are compared. It is shown that when the op amps are modeled with one dominant pole, their frequency responses differ significantly. The importance of switch phasing is emphasized and explained, and GB effects on SC filters are discussed. A quasi-optimal SC biquad topology with respect to GB effects is described. Its performance is illustrated by means of a root-locus plot. This plot allows the designer to determine the ω0 and Q deviations for different values of GB/ω0.

articleTitle: Volterra series analysis of intermodulation distortion in second-order active filters
abstract: The nonlinear performance of second-order active filters using single and two operational amplifiers at high frequencies and/or large-signal levels is investigated. A general procedure using the Volterra series is presented to allow comparison of different filter types regarding intermodulation distortion, and to provide means for improvement. Experimental and theoretical results compare favorably, demonstrating the accuracy of the analysis technique. It is shown that intermodulation distortion for single amplifier filters is much larger than for two-amplifier circuits.

This year, more so than others, time seems to be flying by at a supernatural rate. I was convinced, for example, that my calendar was committing an act of perjury when it indicated that the time had come to write this second President's Report. After all, only yesterday I was mainlining coffee and burning the midnight oil to write my first report. The phrase often invoked to explain this illusion is “time flies when you're having fun.” I must say that these are exciting times for the Circuits and Systems Society and that I have enjoyed my first half year as the Society President.

I assume the office of President with much enthusiasm and optimism that 1983 will be another outstanding year for the Circuits and Systems Society. Before I get too involved with Society business, I would like to express my deep appreciation to Bede Liu for giving us the benefit of his sound leadership, profound vision, and dedicated service as last year's President. I have promised Bede that I will call upon him frequently for advice and keep him very busy as he serves as Past-President.

Throughout this particularly hot and humid summer, certainly one deserving of heavier than normal doses of sea shore lazing and Tom Collins sipping, I have been most impressed by the number of CAS members who've devoted their valuable time to serving the Society. As a consequence, this has been an especially productive summer for the CAS Society.

We have now had our last Board of Directors meeting for 1982. Before reading this, you will have heard the results of various elections including especially Joe Cruz's reelection as IEEE Vice-President for Technical Activities; I won't devote more space here to reporting on these matters.

It is shown that past and current CAD algorithm development for IC design has focused on meeting the challenges of the day, rather than on the needs of the perceivable future. It is argued that new tools required by an emerging technology should be available as soon as the technology is available. Consequently, work on the tools must begin while the technology is being developed. This is not an unrealistic goal, since all major mainframe computers have their operating systems and compilers under development while prototype hardware is being built in the laboratory.

In one of my previous reports, I boasted that 1983 is a banner year for CAS-sponsored conferences. Since this statement was written just after the very successful ISC AS '83, my crystal ball and wishbone were my only connections to ICCAD '83 and ICCD '83. Now that ICCAD '83 and ICCD '83 are behind us, I can report that both were overwhelmingly successful; both had excellent technical programs and drew over 1000 enthusiastic attendees each. I can say, without too much fear of contradiction that the degrees of success achieved at ICCAD '83 and ICCD '83 were somewhat greater than many of us anticipated. I would like to congratulate John Golembeski and Bill McCalla (ICCAD '83), Guy Rabbat and Hal Carter (ICCD '83), and their respective committees for their marvelous successes.

articleTitle: Observations on the evolution of switched capacitor circuits
abstract: Some of the key developments in the theory and practice of switched capacitor circuits are discussed. Emphasis is placed on the sequence of important technological breakthroughs that helped advance the state of the art in this field. CAD software for switched-capacitor circuits is considered, and future developments are discussed.

articleTitle: Recent advances in the application of graph theory to networks
abstract: An in-depth account is given of a relatively small part of applied graph theory that is closely related to electric networks. Two areas are considered in this survey: graph decomposition and hybrid analysis of electrical networks, and flows in communications networks. The latter includes maximum flows with gains and minimal cost flows; multiconnectivity flows; and multiterminal flows in communications nets.

In the March 1983 issue of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Magazine, the new Constitution and Bylaws as passed by the Administrative Committee was published. Because of time delays in the system, we submitted the material for publication at the same time it was submitted to the Technical Activities Board for approval. Unfortunately, some of our sister societies objected to the modifications of the field of interest of the Society. They felt that the wording gave us certain license with their basic areas. As a consequence, a committee was appointed to work out a field of interest which covered our Society's field and did not give us license to invade the territory of others. This modified field of interest has subsequently been approved by the Administrative Committee of the Society. We publish it here for comments by members. If two percent of the members object, we must have a mail vote of the Society.

Dr. Franklin H. Branin, Jr., an IEEE Fellow since 1973, died on November 29, 1982 after a brief illness. He was a member of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. Dr. Branin lived in Woodstock, NY, and was employed as a senior engineer at the IBM Development Laboratory in Kingston, NY. He was 62 years old at the time of his death.

The 1983 IEEE International Conference on Computer-Aided Design, formerly IEEE ICCC82, will be held in Santa Clara, the heart of Silicon Valley and the San Francisco Bay Area, on September 12–14, 1983. Papers will cover design and methodologies, CAD systems, simulation techniques, verification, testing, interactive graphics, design automation, and distributed computing.

Alan Willson, professor of engineering and former assistant dean for graduate studies at UCLA, is honored today for his exceptional record as an engineering educator, researcher, and academic administrator. He is responsible for establishing UCLA's present undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum and has developed three graduate programs which contribute significantly to the Ph.D. program. As assistant dean, he maintained and improved UCLA's high academic standards, established a graduate student orientation program, and made important improvements in the university's fellowship and recruitment programs. ASEE is pleased to present Dr. Will-son with the George Westinghouse Award.

On February 1, 1983, my close friend and colleague Anatol Ivan Zverev died suddenly of a heart attack while watching Mstislav Rostropovich conduct the National Symphony Orchestra at the Kennedy Center in Washington. His main interest during his career was filters, as evidenced by his book, Handbook of Filter Synthesis. He published about 30 papers in the English language in the area of network theory and I had the good fortune of co-authoring the book Filtering in the Time and Frequency Domains with him.

The Swiss Technical University, Zurich, Switzerland, conferred on Dr. Eliahu I. Jury, Professor of Electrical Engineering, University of Miami, Florida; and Professor Emeritus, University of California, Berkeley, the honorary degree of Doctor in the Technical Sciences. The degree was awarded in recognition of his distinguished scientific accomplishments as researcher and teacher in the area of system theory — especially the theory of sampled data systems and stability theory — and in recognition of his services to research in these areas at the ETH Zurich.

articleTitle: Amendment to the constitution and bylaws
abstract: The Circuits and Systems Society is governed by a Constitution and Bylaws, as are the entire IEEE and all of the other technical societies. We have not made a major change in the Constitution and Bylaws since 1972. The field of interest has been out of date. The officer arrangement was not sufficiently flexible to allow for officers among our many members in Europe and the Far East. There was also a number of other minor items not in accordance with present day operation of the Society. We needed to account for more than one Transactions and to align our technical committees with the active committees we now have.
